passage: Forty minutes before judging, the extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark. Vasudha, who had built the circuit, went silent, eyes on the floor. Mohit had seen others snap, "Look at me, what's wrong?" He didn't. He crouched beside the table, not too close, and spoke slowly. "The lights are off. I think it's the cord. Do you want to say it, or write it?" The hall buzzed; the loudspeaker crackled. He slid a pair of earmuffs across the table. "My sister's. Use them if you want." Vasudha put them on. Ten long seconds passed. Mohit waited. Then she tore a strip of chart paper and wrote three steps. Mohit did them one by one. At the third step, the little street lamps on the model flickered back on.

qa.q: What went wrong forty minutes before judging?
qa.a: The extension cord died and the science-fair model went dark.

qa.q: Why did Mohit not tell Vasudha to look at him?
qa.a: He seemed to understand that forcing eye contact would add stress, and he wanted her to answer in her own way.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices helped most under time pressure?
qa.a: He spoke slowly, asked if she wanted to say or write it, offered earmuffs and waited, so she could give clear steps.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt if Mohit had snapped at her like others?
qa.a: She might have frozen further in the noise and not been able to share the fix she knew.

grounding: It shows a teen who speaks clearly, gives time, respects sensory needs, avoids forcing eye contact and asks how she prefers to communicate.

passage: Before the colony Holi, Swati heard that the new boy in C-block, Pranav, didn't like being touched. On the morning itself she saw him at the edge of the park in big headphones, watching the dhol from far away. Her friends were already running at him with fistfuls of pink. "Wait," Swati said, stepping between them. She stopped an arm's length off and didn't try to catch his eye. "Happy Holi. Colour, or no colour?" He said nothing. She waited, counting drumbeats. Finally he held out his phone. He had typed: No colour. Gujiya yes. "Gujiya coming," she said, and went to fetch a plate. When she came back, he had moved one step closer to the party. He typed again: You can text me. It's easier.

qa.q: What did Pranav type the first time?
qa.a: No colour. Gujiya yes.

qa.q: What does Pranav moving one step closer suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt safer and more welcome once Swati respected his space and his answer.

qa.q: What was the key choice Swati made when her friends ran at Pranav?
qa.a: She stepped between them, stood back, asked instead of assuming, and waited for his answer.

qa.q: If you were Pranav, what would you want from the other children at Holi?
qa.a: I would want them to ask first, not throw colour or grab me, and to let me answer by text if that is easier.

grounding: It shows a teen who respects sensory needs and personal space, gives time to answer and learns how another person prefers to communicate.

passage:
"Zubin, we're project partners," Bidisha said, sitting one seat away, not facing him. "How do you like to plan: talking, or writing it out?"
Zubin looked at the desk. A long pause.
Bidisha waited.
"Writing. Shared document."
"Perfect. Do you want the library room? The canteen's loud."
"Yes. The library."
Later, in the library room, Zubin typed fast. "The bridge model should use triangles. Triangles don't bend."
"That's brilliant. Can you explain it in the presentation, or should I?"
"You speak. I'll hold the model."
"Deal." Bidisha didn't offer a high-five; she gave him a thumbs-up across the table instead. Zubin gave one back.

qa.q: Why did Zubin say the bridge model should use triangles?
qa.a: He said triangles don't bend.

qa.q: How did Bidisha seem to feel when Zubin explained the triangles?
qa.a: She seemed delighted and impressed, calling his idea brilliant and inviting him to choose his part.

qa.q: Which choices made Bidisha a good partner?
qa.a: She asked how Zubin liked to communicate, gave him time, offered a quieter room, did not force eye contact and let him choose his role.

qa.q: What would change if Bidisha had insisted on talking face to face in the canteen?
qa.a: Zubin might have felt overwhelmed by noise and pressure, and his clever idea about triangles might never have come out.

grounding: Shows a young person speaking clearly, giving time, respecting sensory needs and asking how a classmate prefers to communicate, with a good effect.

passage: I'm Tejas, and when I was fifteen I captained our school robotics team. I got a lot wrong with Devika at first. She was new, she barely looked at anyone, and I kept saying, "Look at me when I'm explaining." She would go quiet for the rest of the session. Then I noticed she understood wiring better than any of us. So I changed. I spoke slower and gave her time. I asked her how she preferred to get instructions, and she said, "Messages, please." I turned down the buzzer on the test board because she flinched every time. Within a month, Devika was leading the wiring. I learnt that she wasn't broken. I had just been talking to her in the wrong way.

qa.q: How did Devika say she preferred to get instructions?
qa.a: She said, "Messages, please."

qa.q: What did Tejas feel on realising the mistake with Devika?
qa.a: Tejas seems regretful about the early demands and then respectful, recognising that Devika was never broken.

qa.q: What changes helped Devika take part fully?
qa.a: Speaking slowly, giving time, sending messages as she preferred and turning down the buzzer that made her flinch.

qa.q: How might the robotics sessions have felt for Devika before the captain changed?
qa.a: They probably felt stressful and unwelcoming, being told to look at someone and going quiet for the rest of each session.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to speak clearly, give time, respect sensory needs and ask how a teammate prefers to communicate, without treating difference as defect.

passage:
Coach's note, junior swim squad, week 4.
Vaibhav, 14, used to leave the pool deck twenty minutes early. I finally asked him why. He said the whistle and the echo "hurt inside my head." I asked what would help. We agreed: earplugs are fine, I will write each set on the whiteboard instead of shouting it, and I will signal the start with a raised hand. I stopped doing team high-fives with him; he taps the wall instead, which he said he likes.
Result: this week he stayed the full session and knocked two seconds off his time. His mother said he talked about swimming all the way home. Next: ask Ritu, our assistant, to learn the hand signals too.

qa.q: How did the coach signal the start after talking with Vaibhav?
qa.a: The coach signalled the start with a raised hand.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about the whistle and echo at the pool?
qa.a: He felt pained and uncomfortable; he said they hurt inside his head, which is why he used to leave early.

qa.q: What made the coach's response mature and effective?
qa.a: The coach asked Vaibhav what would help, allowed earplugs, wrote sets on the board and dropped forced high-fives, respecting his needs.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's mother feel hearing him talk about swimming all the way home?
qa.a: She is likely glad and relieved to see him enjoying the sport after weeks of him leaving early.

grounding: Shows an adult respecting sensory needs, not forcing physical contact, and asking how a teenager prefers to communicate, with a good effect.

passage:
Thursday night
Chinmay joined our class two weeks ago. Everyone thinks he's rude because he doesn't look at you and never high-fives. Today at the lab table I asked him, "What's the easiest way for you to talk?" He took a long time. I waited. I counted to ten in my head and did NOT fill the silence.
Then he said, "Writing. And no touching, please."
So I wrote my question on the corner of the worksheet. He wrote back a whole paragraph about the reaction! He knows so much.
When the bell rang, he covered his ears. I didn't make a joke. I just said "bye" clearly and didn't wait for him to look up.
I really like him. I want to be the kind of friend who asks first.
Preeti

qa.q: How long did Preeti count in her head while waiting?
qa.a: Preeti counted to ten and did not fill the silence.

qa.q: What does Preeti's last line suggest about how Preeti feels?
qa.a: It suggests Preeti feels warm affection for Chinmay and admiration for how much he knows, and hopes to be a friend who asks first.

qa.q: What did Preeti do well, and why did it help?
qa.a: Preeti asked how Chinmay prefers to communicate, gave time to answer and respected his wish for no touching, so he could share his knowledge comfortably.

qa.q: How might Chinmay experience the lab lesson?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and respected, since he didn't have to force eye contact or high-fives and could talk in writing.

grounding: Preeti speaks clearly, waits for answers, respects Chinmay's sensory needs and asks how he prefers to communicate instead of treating difference as a defect.
